title: Hyperparameter Tuning & Validation: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on parameters vs hyperparameters, validation strategies, search methods, early stopping and nested cross-validation. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Parameters vs Hyperparameters and the Validation Set
points: Parameters are learned from data during training (weights, biases, tree split thresholds); hyperparameters are set before training and control how learning happens (learning rate, depth, regularisation strength, k)
Mental model: training fits parameters on the train set; tuning picks hyperparameters by score on the validation set; the test set is touched once at the end for the final estimate
Three-way split: train (fit parameters), validation (choose hyperparameters), test (unbiased final report); typical 60/20/20 or 70/15/15
Comparison: parameters are optimised by gradient descent or closed form; hyperparameters are found by search because the loss is not differentiable with respect to them

Interview Point: Why can't you tune on the test set? Because repeated selection leaks test information and the score becomes optimistically biased. What is the role of the validation set? It is a proxy for unseen data used only to compare hyperparameter settings.

chapters.title: Cross-Validation Workflow
points: k-fold CV: split train data into k folds, train on k-1 and validate on the held-out fold, rotate k times, average the k scores (k=5 or 10 is the common choice)

Use StratifiedKFold for classification so each fold keeps the class ratio; use TimeSeriesSplit for temporal data so validation always comes after training in time; use GroupKFold when rows share a group (same patient or user)
Everyday usage: cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring='f1') returns one score per fold; report mean and std
Leave-one-out CV is k=n: nearly unbiased but high variance and very expensive; use it only for tiny datasets
Mistake: fitting scaler, imputer or feature selection on all data before splitting leaks information; wrap preprocessing and model in a Pipeline so it is refit inside each fold

Interview Point: Why average over k folds instead of one split? It reduces variance of the estimate. When would plain KFold be wrong? With imbalanced classes, time order or grouped rows. How does a Pipeline prevent leakage? Preprocessing is fitted only on each fold's training part.

chapters.title: Grid Search vs Random Search
points: Grid search tries every combination in a discrete grid: cost multiplies across parameters (3 values x 4 values x 5 values = 60 configs, times k folds)
Random search samples n_iter configurations from distributions; Bergstra and Bengio showed it beats grid when only a few hyperparameters really matter, since each trial tests a new value of every one
Usage: GridSearchCV(est, param_grid, cv=5, scoring=..., n_jobs=-1) and RandomizedSearchCV(est, param_distributions, n_iter=50, cv=5, random_state=0); read best_params_, best_score_, and cv_results_
Sample scale-type hyperparameters on a log scale (learning rate, C, alpha: loguniform(1e-4, 1)); sample integers like depth uniformly

Mistake: a grid that is too fine wastes budget and one that is too narrow misses the optimum; if best_params_ sits on the grid edge, extend the range; keep refit=True so the best model is retrained on the full training data

Interview Point: Why does random search often beat grid search? Low effective dimensionality: few hyperparameters matter, and random sampling gives more distinct values of each. How do you pick the sampling scale? Log scale for hyperparameters spanning orders of magnitude.

chapters.title: Bayesian Optimisation and Early Stopping
points: Bayesian optimisation builds a surrogate model (Gaussian process or TPE) of score vs hyperparameters from past trials, then uses an acquisition function (expected improvement, UCB) to pick the next trial

Loop: fit surrogate to trials so far, maximise acquisition to choose next config, evaluate it, add result, repeat; the acquisition balances exploration (uncertain regions) against exploitation (promising regions)

Comparison with random search: Bayesian is sequential and sample-efficient, best when each trial is expensive (deep nets, large data); random is trivially parallel and a strong baseline; common tools are Optuna (TPE), Hyperopt and scikit-optimize

Early stopping: monitor validation loss each epoch, stop when it has not improved for patience epochs, and restore the best weights; it acts as regularisation and saves compute, with the epoch count effectively tuned automatically

Mistakes: patience too small stops on noise; early stopping on the same set you report the score on gives a biased result, so keep a separate test set; Optuna pruners can also kill bad trials early (MedianPruner)

Interview Point: What does the acquisition function do? It trades exploration against exploitation to choose the next trial. When is Bayesian optimisation not worth it? When trials are cheap and highly parallel. Why is early stopping a regulariser? It limits effective model complexity by halting before overfitting.

chapters.title: Nested Cross-Validation
points: Problem: the best CV score from a hyperparameter search is optimistically biased, because the same folds both select and score the model

Nested CV: an outer loop (e.g. 5 folds) estimates generalisation; inside each outer training split, an inner loop (e.g. 3 folds) runs the full hyperparameter search; the outer test fold is never seen by the search
Usage: inner = GridSearchCV(est, grid, cv=3); scores = cross_val_score(inner, X, y, cv=5); the mean is the honest performance estimate of the whole procedure (search included)
Cost is outer_k x inner_k x configs fits (5 x 3 x 20 = 300 fits), so use random search or a smaller inner loop

Nested CV estimates how well the tuning procedure generalises and does not produce the final model; afterwards run the search once on all training data to get the deployed model, and use plain CV when you only need to compare configs

Interview Point: Why is the plain CV score from a search biased? Selection on the same folds that score it. What do the outer and inner loops each do? The outer estimates performance and the inner selects hyperparameters. Which hyperparameters do you deploy after nested CV? Re-run the search on all training data.

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Tuning and Validation
points: Table: parameters learned by training vs hyperparameters set before; train fits, validation tunes, test reports once
Table of splitters: KFold, StratifiedKFold (imbalanced), TimeSeriesSplit (temporal), GroupKFold (grouped), LOO (tiny data)
Table of search methods: grid (small, discrete), random (default baseline, log-scale), Bayesian/Optuna (expensive trials, sequential)
Code: Pipeline + RandomizedSearchCV(n_iter=50, cv=5) then cross_val_score(search, X, y, cv=5) for nested CV
Top mistakes: preprocessing outside the Pipeline, tuning on test data, grid edge optimum, tiny patience, reporting the search's best CV score as the final estimate

Interview Point: What is the one-sentence workflow? Split off test, tune on train with CV inside a Pipeline, stop early on validation loss, estimate honestly with nested CV, and score the test set once.
